title: Long-Term Adaptations and Detraining Effects of Blood Flow Restriction (BFR) Training
summary:
Blood flow restriction training (BFR training) is a method in which cuffs are applied to reduce arterial blood flow to the working muscles and restrict venous return. This technique is typically combined with low external loads and used in resistance training. In recent years, studies have also examined the application of BFR cuffs in other settings. Notably, even very light loads are sufficient to induce significant increases in muscle strength and muscle mass, comparable to the outcomes of traditional high-load resistance training. The underlying mechanisms responsible for these effects are not yet fully understood. Existing evidence on BFR training predominantly focuses on acute and medium-term effects, especially gains in muscle strength and hypertrophy, with intervention durations usually lasting only a few weeks to a maximum of 16 weeks.

The aim of the proposed project is therefore the systematic and prospective investigation of the long-term health-related and performance-related effects of six months of regular BFR training in comparison to traditional high-load resistance training. In addition, the study will examine the extent to which training-induced adaptations are maintained after a subsequent four-week detraining period.

Methods
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group will perform BFR-Training twice per week for six months. The other group will train over the same period with higher loads and without cuffs. After the six-month training phase, all participants will undergo a four-week detraining period to assess the retention of previously achieved adaptations.
Across the study period, assessments will be conducted at four time points to capture both structural changes (such as alterations in muscle and tendon characteristics) and functional changes (such as muscle strength). In addition, measurements of blood flow in the arms and legs will be performed. This approach will allow identification of how the body responds to each training method and which adaptations persist after the detraining phase.
conditions: Healthy adults without existing disease; investigation of training-related physiological adaptations.

interventions.name:
Low-Load Blood Flow Restriction Training (LL-BFR; Intervention Group)

Training Protocol:

High-Load Resistance Training (HL-RT; Control Intervention)

Training Protocol:

Training load: 70% of the estimated one-repetition maximum (e1RM).
Training volume: 4 sets per exercise with 1 repetition in reserve (1 RIR); a maximum of 12 repetitions is performed in the first set.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Healthy adults without acute or chronic diseases
-No regular use of medication (if medication is taken, prior clarification is required)
-No resistance training within the 6 weeks prior to study initiation
-No additional resistance training during the entire study period
Exclusion criteria:
-Injuries or chronic diseases
-Pre-existing venous conditions (e.g., varicose veins, vascular surgery of the extremities, limbs with dialysis access)
-Arterial hypertension
-Circulatory and coagulation disorders (e.g., history of transient ischemic attack, stroke, angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, peripheral arterial occlusive disease)
-Use of medication (if medication is taken, prior clarification is required)
